title: Who Eats Whom? A Parent Guide
endLine: Food webs show how energy moves through overlapping food chains.

scenes.tts: Why does a hawk need grass? In about thirty minutes, picture cards and yarn let your child see the answer. They practice looking closely, sorting living things, and testing a guess by hand.
scenes.caption: Why does a hawk need grass? In about thirty minutes, picture cards and yarn let your child see the answer. They practice looking closely, sorting living things, and testing a guess by hand.
scenes.visual: Top-down schematic drawing of a warm cream tabletop mat. Friendly hand-drawn cards for grass (left) and a hawk (right) sit beneath a softly pulsing sun card. Blades of grass sway gently while a soft dotted question arc links the grass card to the hawk card.
scenes.narration: Why does a hawk need grass? In about thirty minutes, picture cards and yarn let your child see the answer. They practice looking closely, sorting living things, and testing a guess by hand.

scenes.visual: The grass and hawk cards glide gently toward the edges of the same cream mat as a clean title banner fades in at center: 'Who Eats Whom?' with subtitle 'Parent Guide'. Soft sunlight motes drift slowly across the frame.

scenes.tts: Gather twelve to eighteen index cards or paper squares, crayons or markers, and a ball of yarn. You also need tape or paper clips, a clear floor or table, and scissors just for you. Review the yarn safety rules before you start.
scenes.caption: Gather twelve to eighteen index cards or paper squares, crayons or markers, and a ball of yarn. You also need tape or paper clips, a clear floor or table, and scissors just for you. Review the yarn safety rules before you start.
scenes.visual: On the same cream mat, schematic flat-lay drawings of blank index cards, colorful crayons and markers, a red yarn ball, tape, paper clips, and adult scissors arrange neatly around a clear open center, each highlighting gently as named.
scenes.narration: Gather twelve to eighteen index cards or paper squares, crayons or markers, and a ball of yarn. You also need tape or paper clips, a clear floor or table, and scissors just for you. Review the yarn safety rules before you start.

scenes.tts: Draw cards for sun, grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, and hawk. Line them up in that order. Ask, "Where does the grass go when the grasshopper eats it?" Point the arrow toward the grasshopper. The first arrow shows sunlight reaching the grass.
scenes.caption: Draw cards for sun, grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, and hawk. Line them up in that order. Ask, "Where does the grass go when the grasshopper eats it?" Point the arrow toward the grasshopper. The first arrow shows sunlight reaching the grass.
scenes.visual: Show the adult and child drawing and arranging the six labeled cards. Place a gold arrow from sun to grass. Zoom in as the paper arrow from grass to grasshopper lands pointing to the grasshopper. Then add the remaining arrows toward frog, snake, and hawk.
scenes.narration: Draw cards for sun, grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, and hawk. Line them up in that order. Ask, "Where does the grass go when the grasshopper eats it?" Point the arrow toward the grasshopper. The first arrow shows sunlight reaching the grass.

scenes.tts: Grass makes food using sunlight. Animals are consumers. Mushrooms break down dead material. For the Bay chain, draw sun, phytoplankton, zooplankton, and menhaden, in that order. From menhaden, point an arrow to striped bass and another to osprey.
scenes.caption: Grass makes food using sunlight. Animals are consumers. Mushrooms break down dead material. For the Bay chain, draw sun, phytoplankton, zooplankton, and menhaden, in that order. From menhaden, point an arrow to striped bass and another to osprey.
scenes.visual: Highlight the grass card as a producer and each land animal as a consumer. Briefly show the mushroom with a dead leaf. Along the same mat, show the four named Bay cards in sequence. Animate each arrow, then show two arrows leaving menhaden, one to striped bass and one to osprey.
scenes.narration: Grass makes food using sunlight. Animals are consumers. Mushrooms break down dead material. For the Bay chain, draw sun, phytoplankton, zooplankton, and menhaden, in that order. From menhaden, point an arrow to striped bass and another to osprey.

scenes.tts: Add rabbit, mouse, fox, mushroom, and earthworm cards. Each person holds one to three cards. Start at grass and pass yarn from food to eater. Link living cards to mushroom and earthworm too. The overlapping chains make a food web.
scenes.caption: Add rabbit, mouse, fox, mushroom, and earthworm cards. Each person holds one to three cards. Start at grass and pass yarn from food to eater. Link living cards to mushroom and earthworm too. The overlapping chains make a food web.
scenes.visual: Curving the land cards into a circle on the same mat, show open hands holding yarn loosely. Show strands from grass to grasshopper, rabbit, and mouse. Show grasshopper to frog, frog to snake or hawk, mouse to snake, fox, or hawk, and rabbit to fox or hawk. Show the separate dead-material links to mushroom and earthworm.
scenes.narration: Add rabbit, mouse, fox, mushroom, and earthworm cards. Each person holds one to three cards. Start at grass and pass yarn from food to eater. Link living cards to mushroom and earthworm too. The overlapping chains make a food web.

scenes.tts: Have the snake holder give one gentle tug. Ask anyone who feels it to raise a hand. Now look at the grass card. Ask, "If we take out the grass, who loses a food link first?"
scenes.caption: Have the snake holder give one gentle tug. Ask anyone who feels it to raise a hand. Now look at the grass card. Ask, "If we take out the grass, who loses a food link first?"
scenes.visual: Show the snake holder gently tug a loose strand. Show a raised hand beside the circle. Then highlight the still-connected grass card. Display the question 'If we take out the grass, who loses a food link first?' Keep the full web visible.
scenes.narration: Have the snake holder give one gentle tug. Ask anyone who feels it to raise a hand. Now look at the grass card. Ask, "If we take out the grass, who loses a food link first?"

scenes.visual: Hold the same question and show the grass card still in place. Let a quiet timer ring fill during the four-and-a-half-second silent pause.

scenes.tts: Take out the grass card. Trace the links to grasshopper, rabbit, and mouse first. Then follow their links to other animals. The yarn shows which cards connect. Place a tadpole near producers. Most tadpoles eat algae and plant bits. Adult frogs eat insects.
scenes.caption: Take out the grass card. Trace the links to grasshopper, rabbit, and mouse first. Then follow their links to other animals. The yarn shows which cards connect. Place a tadpole near producers. Most tadpoles eat algae and plant bits. Adult frogs eat insects.
scenes.visual: Lift the grass card and highlight the three links that met it. Then trace the still-visible links from grasshopper, rabbit, and mouse to their eaters. Add a tadpole card beside the producer cards.
scenes.narration: Take out the grass card. Trace the links to grasshopper, rabbit, and mouse first. Then follow their links to other animals. The yarn shows which cards connect. Place a tadpole near producers. Most tadpoles eat algae and plant bits. Adult frogs eat insects.

scenes.tts: Stay with your child the whole time and do all the cutting. Hold yarn loosely. Keep it off necks. Never wrap it tightly around fingers or wrists. Hand the ball over. Stay still while holding yarn. Clear yarn and loose cards before anyone moves. If you work outside, wash hands with soap and water afterward.
scenes.caption: Stay with your child the whole time and do all the cutting. Hold yarn loosely. Keep it off necks. Never wrap it tightly around fingers or wrists. Hand the ball over. Stay still while holding yarn. Clear yarn and loose cards before anyone moves. If you work outside, wash hands with soap and water afterward.
scenes.visual: Show an adult doing the cutting. In the tabletop circle, show an open hand with a loose yarn strand, then the ball passed hand to hand. Show the adult gathering yarn and loose cards before anyone stands. End with a drawing of hands being washed with soap and water.
scenes.narration: Stay with your child the whole time and do all the cutting. Hold yarn loosely. Keep it off necks. Never wrap it tightly around fingers or wrists. Hand the ball over. Stay still while holding yarn. Clear yarn and loose cards before anyone moves. If you work outside, wash hands with soap and water afterward.

scenes.tts: Yarn, string, tape, paper clips, marker caps, and small crayon pieces can be choking hazards. Keep them away from children under four. Call nine one one if choking.
scenes.caption: Yarn, string, tape, paper clips, marker caps, and small crayon pieces can be choking hazards. Keep them away from children under four. Call nine one one if choking.
scenes.visual: On the same mat, show an adult moving the small supplies and wound yarn out of reach. Display the label 'Choking hazard: under four.'
scenes.narration: Yarn, string, tape, paper clips, marker caps, and small crayon pieces can be choking hazards. Keep them away from children under four. Call nine one one if choking.

scenes.tts: Through this game, your child practices asking what happens next and checking a guess against real links. By the end, one gentle tug shows why a hawk still needs sunlight and grass.
scenes.caption: Through this game, your child practices asking what happens next and checking a guess against real links. By the end, one gentle tug shows why a hawk still needs sunlight and grass.
scenes.visual: The full circular yarn web fills the cream mat again. Warm golden energy pulses softly from the sun card into the grass card, then ripples smoothly outward along every red yarn strand all the way to the hawk card.
scenes.narration: Through this game, your child practices asking what happens next and checking a guess against real links. By the end, one gentle tug shows why a hawk still needs sunlight and grass.
